5.0.0.en: 1 Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil. 2 Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few. 3 For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words. 4 When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. 5 Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay. 6 Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands? 7 For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God.

5.0.1.en: If the world apart from God is vanity and a seizing of the wind, then all the more is formal worship outside the sphere of the Spirit vanity and a seizing of the wind. Here the Preacher begins to apply our sincere view of life to worship, whether communal or private.

5.0.2.en: a. A call to enter the house of God:

5.0.3.en: "Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil" [1].

5.0.4.en: God created the world good, that the whole earth might be like the house of God, in which every man would meet his beloved, holy Creator in a spirit of love, praise and joy. But when sin entered the world the world became vanity, the earth brought forth thorns and thistles, and man felt a dryness toward his good Creator. Yet God, in His love for man, allowed him to build a house for Him as an icon of the eternal heaven, to which the believers may flee while they are still in this world, so that the Spirit of God carries their hearts, thoughts, wills, feelings and senses to what is above the visible world and above time... Therefore we do not wonder that the Preacher, after affirming the vanity of the world, began his counsels to man with going to the house of God. In other words the Preacher says: Flee from the passing world to its eternal Creator by entering His holy house and meeting Him in the sphere of love and obedience.

5.0.5.en: The Psalmist knew how to flee to God's sanctuaries in times of distress, to experience God's mercies and the riches of His grace:

5.0.6.en: "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever" (Ps 23:6).

5.0.7.en: "Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident. One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple" (Ps 27:3-4).

5.0.8.en: "For thou hast been a shelter for me... I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings" (Ps 61:3-4).

5.0.9.en: "All the day long have I been plagued... Until I went into the sanctuary of God" (Ps 73:14, 17).

5.0.10.en: Thus when the Psalmist felt troubles, outward or inward, he found a refuge in the house of the Lord, where he meets God Himself, his Savior. He lifts him up to His graces and grants him the experience of the beauty of the heavenly life, so that he is no longer occupied with the afflictions that time brought him. In the house of the Lord he finds God the King seated on the throne, so he does not fear if a host encamps against him or war rises against him!

5.0.11.en: However, entering the house of the Lord and dwelling in it requires purity and holiness of heart, so that the believer may dwell with the holy God in His sanctuary and have fellowship with Him... Therefore he says: "Keep thy foot" [1].

5.0.12.en: b. What does keeping the foot when going to the house of the Lord mean, but what the wise man says: "The prudent man looketh well to his going" (Prov 14:15), and also: "Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established. Turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove thy foot from evil" (Prov 4:26). It is as though he says: You are walking the royal road to enter the throne of the King of kings; take care lest you swerve by a blow from the right, that is, by self-righteousness, or by a blow from the left, that is, by falling into evil. Enter the house of the Lord with your heart before your body... Do not hasten with the steps of your bodily feet, but enter with your depths, led by the Holy Spirit of God.

5.0.13.en: Some see in this commandment, "Keep thy foot," a reference to God's command to the prophet Moses and to Joshua the son of Nun to take off their shoes from their feet (Ex 3:5; Josh 5:15), and as Origen says, it is a call to take off the shoe made of the skin of dead animals. We put off from us whatever touches the dead life, or the works of the old man, that we may live by the Spirit of God in newness of life. Also it is made from the skin of drums, which give a loud sound without work, as though the taking off of the skin were a call to reject vainglory and the love of display...

5.0.14.en: Let us enter the house of the Lord with our hearts after taking the shoes off them, that we may enjoy the works of the new man, so that we do not walk in the evil life nor seek self-righteousness, but listen to the voice of God and obey Him with a holy and pure will, for to hear God is better than the sacrifice of fools!

5.0.15.en: c. To hear is better than the sacrifice of fools: Keep your heart, or your inner man, in obedience, as the eye that beholds God by faith, and the foot by which you walk toward Him and enjoy your dwelling with Him and His dwelling with you.

5.0.16.en: If life is changing and passing away, and needs vigilance and caution lest you fall into the snares of being entangled in it and tempted to hoard its temporal goods, then all the more, when you turn your heart toward the house of God, you come to know the royal road, the road of obedience to Christ, for to walk by it and in it is greater than offering material gifts to the house of the Lord. Receive the Lord Christ Himself as a royal road, and so bear His righteousness and obedience, offering your heart as a sacrifice of practical love... for God asks for your heart, not your money! And as you give Him your heart poured out in practical love, through your union with the obedient Christ (Heb 5:5), you offer all your life, its greater and lesser sins.

5.0.17.en: He asks us to hear, for the house of God is the house of the divine Word; we hear Him that we may keep Him within us by His Holy Spirit. The first word in the Ten Commandments is "Hear"... for God wants us to enter His house to listen, and to have it kept in the heart and in practical conduct, because hearing means practical obedience.

5.0.18.en: God, as we know Him in the Holy Bible and in the experience of the Church throughout the ages, is the "Hearer of prayers"; He inclines His ear to us, His children, to hear the whispers of our lips and the hidden sighs of our hearts, and we, in our love for Him, answer His listening to us with our listening to Him... We share with Him the quality of "hearing." In His love He comes down to us to hear us, and in His love He also grants us the spirit of obedience so that we hear Him!

5.0.19.en: Hearing (obedience) is not a kind of humiliation, as some think in the pride of their hearts, but it is the mark of the true believer in his fellowship with God who hears our voices... We hear Him in His commandment as in His house, in our hidden prayers and in our dealings with our neighbor... We bear the mark of hearing as a holy nature in the Lord that accompanies us in our closet, in our church, in our homes, in our work, even on the road; we long to hear everyone and obey him, but in the Lord!

5.0.20.en: Finally, by hearing he calls us to heavenly wisdom and a walk in the righteousness of God; wisdom is bound to righteousness as folly is bound to evil, for he says: "the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil." The fool not only sins but sins without caring, whereas the wise man, if he sins, cannot bear his sinful conduct, but accuses himself before God in repentance, asking Him to grant him in practice the mark of "hearing" or "obedience."

5.0.21.en: God rejects the sacrifice of fools because, while they practice the formalities of worship, they refuse to listen inwardly to God's commandments, so that evil reigns over their heart and mind and they do not care about it.

5.0.22.en: * Upon him who hears and obeys, holy peace descends.

5.0.23.en: St. John Saba We can sense how our fathers feared falling under the letter of formalities from what St. John Saba said: [O man of God, how long will only the black (the monastic habit) comfort your soul? Be wholly a flame, and burn those around you, that you may see the beauty hidden within you]. And St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian says: [The garb of good religion is put upon me, but its power is not in me]. [I stand in the front of the church, and I am not worthy to be last in it]. [I withdrew from the world, and I am sunk in it up to my neck in my heart and mind].

5.1.0.en: d. Not multiplying vain words during prayer: "Therefore let thy words be few" [2], for God asks for work and sincerity, not a multitude of vain words" (Mt 6:7). "For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words" [3].

5.1.1.en: Let our prayers be calm, uttered without haste, uttered by our tongue as by our practical life, so that our whole being cries out in the language of practical love, which God listens to and all heaven rejoices in. Perhaps for this reason he says: "Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth" [2]. It is as though he says: Let your life, which is marked by heavenliness, speak and pray, so that the words of prayer rise with it to the divine throne.

5.1.2.en: Perhaps the Preacher wanted the worshiper not to hurry through the words to finish his prayer, but from time to time to lift his mind, heart and feelings toward God, expressing by inward contemplation the depth of his clinging to Him, and in this way leaving room for the grace of God to work in him during prayer... He speaks in the Spirit, listens to the voice of the Lord and sees in the Spirit. Prayer becomes a dialogue of mutual love in which man shares not with his tongue alone but with his whole inner being.

5.1.3.en: He says: "For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth"... Wait in your prayers for the Heavenly One to reveal to you His heavens, to teach you the language of heaven, and to grant you fellowship in praise with the heavenly ones.

5.1.4.en: * Listen to the counsel of the Preacher: Utter not a word before God; for he says that God is in heaven and you are on earth [2]. I believe that by that distance which separates heaven from earth, despite the intimacy of their mutual communion, he shows the nature of God, which immeasurably surpasses the sphere of man's thought. As the stars are far beyond the reach of the fingers, so, and by a far greater degree, that nature which is above all the thoughts of men rises above our earthly thoughts.

5.1.5.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * Silence your tongue that your heart may speak, silence your heart that the Spirit may speak in you.

5.1.6.en: St. John Saba The Preacher calls us not to multiply words in prayer, perhaps so that we may not utter unintelligible words, as the Apostle Paul says: "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also" (1 Cor 14:15). When we pray or praise God we must speak with deliberation and reverence, aware that we are speaking with the Heavenly One...

5.1.7.en: The Preacher does not attack long prayers as long as they are offered with understanding, wisdom and godliness, for the Lord Christ sometimes spent the whole night in prayer (Lk 6:12), and the Apostle asks us to pray without ceasing (1 Thess 5:17), and to pray always (Col 1:3). And it is said of St. Arsenius that he was absorbed in prayer from sunset until sunrise, spending the whole night in the sweetness of converse with God.

5.1.8.en: * Pray and do not grow weary; pray continually a prayer of faith, hope and love...

5.1.9.en: But let not your prayer be in a multitude of words. Our Lord is the first who shortened long speeches, so that in your long prayer to God you may not appear as one who goes on to give Him a lesson.

5.1.10.en: What you need in prayer is godliness, not babbling.

5.1.11.en: When you pray, do not be a babbler like the heathen, who think that they shall be heard for their much speaking (Mt 6:7); be not like them, for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask Him...

5.1.12.en: You will not cease from prayer if you continually seek the happy life...

5.1.13.en: It is said that in Egypt there are brethren who continually offer short petitions recited quickly, in order to preserve the attention (concentration of mind) necessary for everyone who prays.

5.2.0.en: St. Augustine The Preacher cites an example that affirms the importance of work over a multitude of words: "For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words" [3]. Continuous, earnest work engenders happy dreams, or fulfills man's dreams and desires, but the idle talk of many words turns man's life to folly, his words being "a fool's voice." Much business makes a man wise and realistic even in his dreams, while a multitude of words reveals emptiness and folly!

5.2.1.en: e. Seriousness and sincerity in vows:

5.2.2.en: "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools...

5.2.3.en: Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.

5.3.0.en: Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin" [4-6].

5.3.1.en: In our study of the books of Numbers (chapter 30) and Leviticus (chapter 27): (Num 30; Lev 27) we spoke about vows in the Mosaic Law. A vow is a promise to consecrate something to God, which a man is bound to fulfill; it points to an inward longing and a sure desire not for consecrating things but for consecrating the heart itself to God, for the glory of His name and the spread of His Kingdom. It befits the believer to keep what he has uttered and not to break his word (Lev 27:2; Judg 11:35), nor is it fitting to put it off until tomorrow.

5.3.2.en: The Preacher calls those who do not pay their vows or who delay the payment "fools," because they speak foolishly without deliberation, and this is counted a kind of contempt for God. It would have been better for them not to vow than to vow and not pay, so that they would not be counted as breakers of a promise.

5.3.3.en: They speak with their mouth and their flesh sins. Here the flesh means the whole man. Ananias and Sapphira vowed to give the whole price of their field... but they kept back part of the price, and were counted as having lied to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:1-11). Jephthah was hasty in his vow to the Lord to offer as a burnt offering whoever came forth from the doors of his house to meet him... and he offered his only daughter, a virgin, as a burnt offering (Judg 11:30, 34). And Herod promised hastily to give Herodias her request even up to half the kingdom, and the head of St. John the Baptist was cut off!

5.3.4.en: Let us not be hasty in our promises and vows to God and to men!

5.3.5.en: Abba Isaac, in his Conferences with St. John Cassian, sees that the vow is "prayer," saying thus: [If you have offered a prayer to the Lord, do not delay to fulfill it. And we pray when we renounce this world and promise that we will die to all worldly deeds and to the life of this world, and serve the Lord with all the purposes of the heart].

5.3.6.en: Our prayers are vows or pledges... in them we declare our renunciation of the pleasures of the world and our acceptance of the Kingdom of God within us, in them we reject the destructive fatherhood of the devil and accept God's fatherhood to us... Let us fulfill this not in words only but in our practical life by the Holy Spirit of God who works in us, so that we may say with power with the Apostle: "We are not of the night, nor of darkness" (1 Thess 5:5).

5.3.7.en: In our study of the Book of Psalms we noticed that the Psalmist declares his paying of vows by praising God, for there is no vow that gladdens the heart of God like our praising Him and giving Him thanks in the midst of our afflictions and troubles! By this vow we declare that our heavenly God alone is able to bring us into the joyful angelic life and to carry us over the cares and preoccupations of the world!

5.3.8.en: The Preacher continues his discourse on the obligation to fulfill the vow, saying:

5.4.0.en: "Neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error" [6].

5.4.1.en: He means by the angel here the priest (Rev 2:1), for it does not befit the believer to contrive excuses before God's stewards, claiming that what he uttered he did not mean, or that he did not know the truth of his abilities or capacities. For God is angry with those who are hasty in their words and vows [6].

5.4.2.en: The writer gives the cause of this sickness and its remedy, saying:

5.5.0.en: "For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God" [7].

5.5.1.en: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker says: [As a throng of dreams is vain, so is a multitude of words. But the fear of God is man's salvation, though it is hard to acquire].

5.5.2.en: Three things spoil the pledges of our mouth to God: a multitude of dreams, that is, being occupied with illusions without practical, realistic conduct; vanities, that is, being occupied with the affairs of vain life; and a multitude of words. In other words, for our pledges to be holy and realistic we must flee from vain thoughts (dreams), from vain deeds, and from vain words, by setting the fear of God before our eyes when we think, work or speak. Let us fear God, and He will reign over our thoughts, our conduct and our words... and we shall be, in our whole being, witnesses of truth to His work in us!

5.6.0.en: 8 If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they. 9 Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field. 10 He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity. 11 When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what good is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes? 12 The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep. 13 There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. 14 But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand. 15 As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand. 16 And this also is a sore evil, that in all points as he came, so shall he go: and what profit hath he that hath laboured for the wind? 17 All his days also he eateth in darkness, and he hath much sorrow and wrath with his sickness.

5.6.1.en: He asked us for true spiritual worship in the face of the vanity of the world, warning us against dry, literal formalities, and offering us the fear of God as a remedy for our weakness in worship. Now he ties spiritual worship to practical conduct filled with sincere love, offering us also the fear of God as our support so that we do not fear the oppressors, for he says:

5.6.2.en: a. "If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they" [8].

5.6.3.en: May we not marvel at the matter when we see injustice prevailing on the earth, for over against it there is a comforting sight in heaven. God, who is higher than every throne and above every authority, will surely carry out His care for the oppressed and His justice at the right time. If the oppressors are exalted, the glory of God is above the heavens (Ps 113).

5.6.4.en: Perhaps the Preacher feared lest the believer marvel at the sight of injustice prevailing on the earth and himself yield to vanity and walk in a spirit of injustice and oppression, on the pretext that the whole world walks so. Rather he should turn to the one who is higher, that is, to the judges or rulers, and if he finds no one on earth to do justice to the poor and the oppressed, the Heavenly One Himself, higher than all, intervenes.

5.7.0.en: b. If the poor man has become like the earth we do not despise him, for all need him, even the king needs the service of the field and its fruit: "Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field" [9]. All living creation needs the earth... from it the beasts eat, and from it the king eats... so why do we despise it?!

5.7.1.en: Let us give love to our poor brethren and not despise them, even if they have become in the eyes of many earth that they tread on with their feet, for by our love for them and our service to them we ourselves are served and our heart is lifted up to heaven itself!

5.8.0.en: c. Let us love the poor and oppressed brethren even if they have become earth, because they will serve us on the great day of the Lord when we hear: "Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (Mt 25:40). We give them our silver and our possessions, or rather our love, and so we profit eternally; but if we hoard our possessions our souls are not satisfied [10], and we do not profit by them [11], they give us no rest [12], but may even harm us [13]... and they are passing... for they leave us [14] or we leave them against our will [15-16].

5.9.s.en: First: The love of silver is not satisfying:

5.9.0.en: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase" [10].

5.9.1.en: He who cleaves to the Lord through godliness profits greatly: "Godliness with contentment is great gain" (1 Tim 6:6), and as the Apostle says: "every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full..." (Phil 4:18). But he who cleaves to the love of riches and wealth enlarges his soul like hell (Hab 2:5), and the whole world cannot satisfy it. It is like the horseleach, a worm that abounds in marshes and attaches itself to animals, drinking from the marshes and sucking the blood of the animals, clinging very closely to them, which says, "Give, give" (Prov 30:15).

5.9.2.en: * He who loves riches dreams of gold when he sleeps, but to him who loves detachment (the gold) hastens...

5.9.3.en: * The sons of the Kingdom tread on gold like dust, and you now rejoice and do not carry it...

5.9.4.en: * O Lord, he who possesses You, the bread of the day, has no need, for he is richer than all the rich of the whole world.

5.10.s.en: Second: Abundance of riches brings no profit:

5.10.0.en: "When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what good is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes?! [11].

5.10.1.en: As a man grows richer his responsibilities grow, so what does he profit if his heart remains greedy for the love of money while those who work with him eat with gladness and joy?! In other words, while the heart of the rich man burns with the lust for riches and the spirit of covetousness, those who live from his goods are happier than he... they may gain their souls and enjoy eternal riches, while he loses his soul?! Let us give them our love, that we also may profit, and our love for them becomes our eternal wealth.

5.10.2.en: * Be without greed and do not be without mercy. If you are the master of gold, not its servant, you use it well... Greed makes you a slave, and love makes you free.

5.11.s.en: Third: The love of riches robs us of rest:

5.11.0.en: When he compared the rich man, whose heart is not satisfied with the abundance of his goods, with his workers, he found that the workers eat of the goods by their wages, while the rich man may deprive himself of the goods because of his stinginess and love of acquiring, or the workers may enjoy the eating of heavenly food through their godly life while the stingy rich man is deprived of the heavenly table... Someone may say: But the workers toil and labor, while the rich man in ease reaps the fruit of their labor. The Preacher comments on this by saying that although the poor workers labor in body, they enjoy pleasure when they sleep, regardless of the kind of food they eat or its amount, but the greedy rich man's heart finds no rest at night... Sleep flies from his eyes as he thinks how to multiply his wealth... Therefore it was rightly said: "for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Ps 127:2).

5.11.1.en: "The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep" [12].

5.11.2.en: The worker earns his living by toil but sleeps deeply and with pleasure, while being occupied with multiplying wealth brings cares and anxiety...

5.11.3.en: * The poor man, even if he is a slave and unable to fill his belly completely, at least enjoys the refreshment of sleep, but the lust of the rich man is always accompanied by insomnia, sleepless nights and tension of mind. What is more foolish than this...?!

5.11.4.en: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker * The Preacher sees that riches cause their owner troubles, for losing them causes him great anxiety and tension. They are truly as good as lost, for they are left behind here, and are of no use to the dead.

5.11.5.en: St. Ambrose If bodily toil for the necessities of the body gives pleasure to the body at night, how much more does the one who strives spiritually enjoy true pleasure when he labors for the salvation of his soul?! He truly sleeps the sleep of death in sweetness and delight, for he rests from his labors and his works follow him (Rev 14:13).

5.11.6.en: * As sheaves of joy follow those who sow in tears, so joy follows those who have endured hardships for God's sake. Bread gained with much sweat seems sweet to the sowers, and sweet are the works of righteousness to the heart that has received the knowledge of Christ.

5.11.7.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian While he warns us throughout the Book against hoarding or greed, he wishes to affirm that it is also not fitting for us to live in slackness and sluggishness, but to work and strive in our daily life as in our worship, for "the sleep of a labouring man is sweet" [12].

5.12.s.en: Fourth: The love of riches or hoarding is harmful:

5.12.0.en: "There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun.

5.12.1.en: Namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt" [13].

5.12.2.en: The evil the wise man saw under the sun is that a rich man devotes himself to guarding his wealth, and behold it harms him, as he says in another place: "So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof" (Prov 1:19). The problem lies not in wealth but in the greed for gain, for many rich men have been found who gained their souls by not being entangled in wealth.

5.12.3.en: * Abraham was rich, and he is the first of those who sit at table in the Kingdom.

5.12.4.en: * Nor did Joseph incline when he found riches, and riches did not hinder him from the love of God...

5.12.5.en: It was easy for Joseph to walk the lofty, perfect way when he was rich.

5.12.6.en: * Riches are a good creation, which the fool defiles.

5.12.7.en: * It is hard for the rich man to enter into life because of his riches, since he loves them and cares nothing for the Kingdom.

5.13.s.en: Fifth: Riches are passing; they leave us or we leave them:

5.13.0.en: By the very effort the rich man spends to grow richer he is exposed to losing everything he owns through a losing venture... How many rich men have lost all they owned in moments when the financial markets are struck by a sudden worldwide slump?! And how many global companies have been shattered and gone bankrupt because some company declared bankruptcy?!

5.13.1.en: However great the rich man's care for his wealth, suddenly he finds it has slipped from his hands like a bird, and as the wise man says: "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven" (Prov 23:4-5).

5.13.2.en: The rich man may spend all his effort to leave his son a huge inheritance, and behold he leaves him a fortune burdened with debts:

5.13.3.en: "But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand" [14].

5.14.0.en: If he does not lose his wealth but leaves a great inheritance to his son, he himself will leave it: "As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand" [15].

5.14.1.en: * From this world which you have loved you will carry nothing with you, except the vice which you have loved.

5.15.0.en: St. Augustine Finally wise Solomon presents a bitter picture of some greedy rich men who love money, for though they own much they eat all the days of their life in darkness in order to save the consumption of fuel! "All his days also he eateth in darkness, and he hath much sorrow and wrath" [17].

5.16.s.en: 3. Joy and thanksgiving for God's gifts:

5.16.0.en: 18 Behold that which I have seen: it is good and comely for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy the good of all his labour that he taketh under the sun all the days of his life, which God giveth him: for it is his portion. 19 Every man also to whom God hath given riches and wealth, and hath given him power to eat thereof, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labour; this is the gift of God. 20 For he shall not much remember the days of his life; because God answereth him in the joy of his heart.

5.16.1.en: If the lover of riches and hoarding lives as in darkness, fearing lest he consume much fuel... lives in sorrow and wrath, since he does not feel God's care for him and His concern for him, and whatever he receives he murmurs, then the true believer, on the contrary, lives his daily life using everything in his hands with joy, giving thanks to God for His gifts.

5.16.2.en: The writer offered the same counsel at the end of the second chapter, after affirming from his personal experience that sensual pleasures are unable to satisfy his heart (Eccl 2:24-26).

5.16.3.en: His counsel is summed up in the following:

5.16.4.en: a. That man eat and drink and do his work as divine gifts [18].

5.17.0.en: b. That he count riches and wealth also as divine gifts [19].

5.17.1.en: c. That he live his daily life with joy in the Lord [19], for "God answereth him in the joy of his heart" [20], or as some translate it: "because God gives him the desire of his heart as joy."

5.17.2.en: * It is the gift of God that man reap the fruit of his labor with joy... Such a man is not troubled, nor is he enslaved all his life to evil thoughts, but measures his life by good works, for his heart is good in everything, and exults with joy in the gift of God.

5.18.0.en: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker "Because God answereth him in the joy of his heart" [20], meaning that God looks upon the believing man as His beloved child, whom He occupies with heavenly wisdom, the earnest of eternal glory and the knowledge of some mysteries, like one who wishes to gladden his heart. The Evangelist says: "In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit, and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes" (Lk 10:21). This is God's gift to us, His children, of which the wise of this age are deprived. This gift gladdens our heart more than all the riches and wealth of the world!
